cruise-pianist-overboard-rescue.headline: Cruise ship pianist rescued after nine hours in the Pacific
cruise-pianist-overboard-rescue.body_md:
A pianist who works aboard a Royal Caribbean cruise ship was pulled alive from the Pacific off Southern California on Friday. Officials believe he had been in the water for about nine hours. He was taken to hospital in stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC.

The man, a crew member on the *Ovation of the Seas*, has not been publicly identified. Newport Beach lifeguards believe he went overboard at around 2:30am. He was found 15 to 20 miles offshore, near Catalina Island.

## Two fishermen and a lucky find

He was spotted by two fishermen, Grant Garrett and Sean Norton. "Yeah, it's a human being," Garrett said. "Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in."

The Coast Guard said it received a report from a Good Samaritan who had recovered a conscious person from the water. The man was handed over to Newport Beach lifeguards, who confirmed that he worked on the ship.

Norton recalled what the man said to him. "The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" he said. Norton put the time in the water nearer ten hours than nine, so the exact figure is an estimate.

Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda described the location as "pretty much in the middle of the ocean." Norton credited the man's survival partly to warm water of about 76°F (24°C), which he put down to a "crazy super El Niño year." Nine hours in much colder water would be a very different proposition.

## The question nobody has answered yet

The rescue itself is the happy part. The harder question is how a person can go over the side of a ship carrying thousands of people and not be missed for hours.

None of the accounts published so far says when the ship's crew noticed he was gone, or whether any man-overboard procedure was triggered. They also do not explain how he fell. The Coast Guard says it is investigating, and Royal Caribbean Group has said only that it is "providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time." The company has no further details to share, citing his privacy.

That silence matters. Large cruise ships carry overboard-detection technology and operate set search procedures, but a crew member's absence can be easier to overlook than a passenger's. That is a general point, not something established in this case. If this man was missed only when fishermen found him, or if the ship raised the alarm and the response was slow, the story goes beyond one lucky survivor.

## What to watch

The Coast Guard's findings are the next thing to look for. They should show when the ship realised he was missing and what it did next. Until then, the account rests on what two fishermen saw and what a man in the water managed to say.

brand-case-nandy-time-is-up.headline: Russell Brand case: Nandy says 'time is up' on abuse in media
brand-case-nandy-time-is-up.body_md:
Lisa Nandy has told the media industry that “time is up” on the abuse of women, three days after a jury convicted Russell Brand of rape and sexual assault. What the culture secretary has not yet done is attach a rule, a regulator or a deadline to the warning.

Brand was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday 5 November of one count of rape and three of sexual assault. He was acquitted on the remaining counts, including two of rape and one of attempted indecent assault. He denied all the allegations. The convictions relate to incidents between 2004 and 2009: a rape at his home, a groping at a party, an incident at a London radio station, and an assault during an advertisement recording. Mr Justice Bennathan has told him to expect a “significant custodial term”, and he remains in prison pending sentence on Monday. The Metropolitan Police say a separate inquiry into rape allegations by two other women is continuing.

## What Nandy said

Appearing on the BBC’s *Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg* and on Sky News, Nandy was blunt. “Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously,” she said on the BBC. She told Sky that the sector needs “much stronger” protections for women who come forward, and that it is not doing enough.

She also doubted that anyone could claim the abuse “couldn’t happen today”, suggesting it is probably happening now. Asked what had changed in recent years in how institutions help people to speak up, she said she could not see much. Media and entertainment, like politics, carry particular responsibility, she argued: short-term, flexible contracts and steep power imbalances mean that complaining can cost a worker their reputation and their next job.

That last point echoes the testimony. Several complainants said they stayed silent because of Brand’s fame, fear of disbelief or worry for their careers. One told the court the industry “protects its own”. Another said that in 2009 two producers told her Brand would keep working only if she gave him a massage; she complained to her line manager, but said nothing came of it.

## Rhetoric or rulebook?

The concrete ask was modest. Nandy urged media organisations to join the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, an industry body that protects whistleblowers. Joining is voluntary. On anything stronger, she said only that the government is “considering what further steps we can take”.

That leaves the real question open. Reports of her interviews carry no mention of legislation, a timetable, or new duties on broadcasters and producers around complaint handling, vetting or reporting, and Ofcom did not feature. Until ministers name one of those, the statement is a call for self-policing, aimed at an industry that has heard such calls before. Reviews at the BBC and at Banijay, the production group behind some of Brand’s work, followed the 2023 documentary that first aired the allegations. The BBC’s found that staff between 2006 and 2008 felt unable to raise concerns; Banijay’s found no formal complaints had been made. Broadcasters say they have since strengthened duty-of-care protections, though without public specifics.

The pressure may grow. Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley said he “wouldn’t be surprised” if many more people came forward. A US civil suit over an alleged 2010 incident on the set of *Arthur* is also continuing, after a judge rejected Warner Bros’ bid to have it dismissed.

## What to watch

Brand’s sentencing on Monday will set the tone, and a long term would sharpen the question of what the industry did, and did not, do at the time. After that, the test is simple: whether the government’s “further steps” arrive as a consultation, a statutory duty or nothing at all. Nandy, who this week also defended herself against claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday, has now put her name to a promise that can be checked.

floor.headline: One snap-back carries the shadow book; YATO goes nowhere
floor.body_md: A quiet book with one loud trade. HOGS.MI did what the thesis predicted: a deep slide, a sharp rebound, and a take-profit hit with no visible catalyst at either end. That reads as a technical snap-back, not a re-rating, and the distinction matters. YATO.MC was the flatter kind of day. Price went nowhere, the position closed on schedule, and costs took a small bite that the cost floor had already allowed for. Neither the overshoot bet nor the tight stop was tested. The strategy's strong day rests on a single bounce, which makes it a sample of one. Tomorrow's question is whether the next deeply oversold name rebounds the same way, or whether HOGS was the exception that made the results look better than the process.

floor.headline: Shadow book: the bounce paid, but the LLYC.MC stop did the damage
floor.body_md: A shadow book's day in which the winner could not cover the losers. HOGS.MI did what the thesis asked: heavy volume into a capitulation-style flush, then a bounce that reached its target. LLYC.MC did the opposite. Its stop fired on a slide that kept sliding, and the earlier bounce in the name offered no shelter for this entry. HTT closed on schedule at a modest loss, which is the kind of result that looks fine until the schedule is the only reason it ended. The lesson is uncomfortable: a deep, RSI-washed flush may be a bottom or merely the middle of a slide, and nothing in the data says which. Tomorrow's test is whether the mean-reverter keeps sizing into that uncertainty.
